title: Harvey In Practice: How M&A Teams Use Harvey Across the Deal Lifecycle
author: Harvey Team

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s workflow-centred value proposition and materially extends it with a concrete end-to-end M&A diligence workflow plus context-specific time-savings evidence. It supports AI-assisted judgment rather than access or usage volume as the source of value, although its reported firm experience is not an independent accuracy or causal evaluation.
qs: #### In Practice: End-to-End M&A Due Diligence  In the walkthrough below, a transactional lawyer uses Harvey to capture deal documents from email, analyze hundreds of contracts in Vault, and automatically generate a citation-backed red-flags memo for the client.

At GSK Stockmann, using Harvey for structured M&A, private equity, venture capital, and real estate diligence delivered initial time savings of 15-20%, with up to 75% time savings when applied to unstructured data rooms.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the application-layer thesis by describing Harvey embedded across concrete M&A workflows while retaining lawyers’ judgment. Its reported time savings provide positive operational evidence, but as vendor-reported customer results and hypothetical applications they do not establish independent performance or durable defensibility, consistent with the cluster’s qualifications.
qs: By embedding AI directly into the workflows lawyers already use, Harvey fits naturally into the way M&A teams work — helping them save time and focus on the judgment that matters most.

At GSK Stockmann, using Harvey for structured M&A, private equity, venture capital, and real estate diligence delivered initial time savings of 15-20%, with up to 75% time savings when applied to unstructured data rooms.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, task-level deployment by presenting Harvey as an aid for bounded M&A workflows—document review, risk flagging, diligence synthesis and translating deal terms into operational guidance—rather than as a replacement for lawyers. Its claims are mainly prospective and anecdotal, with no comparative performance evidence, quantified gains or substantive treatment of verification and operating-model requirements.

Analyzing sources across the web, Harvey helps lawyers understand a target’s business, history, industry position, ownership structure, and recent developments — while also highlighting potential risks, red flags, or areas that may warrant closer diligence.

kp.k: Diligence automation redirects lawyers toward material risks
kp.d: The Harvey Team describes AI reviewing commercial contracts, employment agreements, compliance policies and environmental reports to identify risks, provisions and unresolved issues. Its illustrated workflow captures documents from email, analyzes hundreds of contracts in Vault and generates a citation-backed client memo. The stated mechanism is prioritizing high-impact issues and senior legal judgment while accelerating transactions.
qs: Harvey can review large volumes of diligence materials — such as commercial contracts, employment agreements, compliance policies, and environmental reports — to surface red flags, material risks, key provisions, and open issues.

In the walkthrough below, a transactional lawyer uses Harvey to capture deal documents from email, analyze hundreds of contracts in Vault, and automatically generate a citation-backed red-flags memo for the client.

kp.k: Customer diligence savings vary with document organization
kp.d: The vendor reports that GSK Stockmann achieved initial time savings of 15-20% in structured M&A, private equity, venture capital and real estate diligence, with up to 75% savings in unstructured data rooms. These are reported customer results; the article supplies no sample size, measurement period or study methodology.
qs: At GSK Stockmann, using Harvey for structured M&A, private equity, venture capital, and real estate diligence delivered initial time savings of 15-20%, with up to 75% time savings when applied to unstructured data rooms.

kp.k: First-pass review augments associates and partner judgment
kp.d: The author says Harvey analyzes purchase agreements and ancillary documents for inconsistencies with terms sheets and deviations from precedent, producing issues lists from redlines and deal-specific suggested revisions. The claimed role change is faster associate review and better-organized negotiation information for partners, explicitly not replacement of legal judgment.
qs: Harvey can analyze purchase agreements and ancillary documents to flag inconsistencies with terms sheets, identify deviations from precedent, and produce structured issues lists from redlined documents where suggested revisions are tailored to the deal context.

This enables associates to move faster on first‑pass review while giving partners a clearer, more organized view of negotiation points, open questions, and risk areas — without replacing legal judgment.

kp.k: Precedent extraction supports reporting and knowledge sharing
kp.d: The article describes lawyers extracting and structuring transaction terms across precedent agreements, including price adjustments, earn-outs, closing conditions, representations, covenants and indemnities. It presents faster reporting, precedent analysis and internal knowledge sharing as the benefits.
qs: M&A lawyers use Harvey to extract and summarize critical deal terms like purchase price adjustments, earn-outs, closing conditions, representations and warranties, covenants, and indemnification packages across precedent transaction agreements.
These structured summaries support faster deal reporting, precedent analysis, and internal knowledge sharing.

kp.k: Completeness checks shift attention toward substantive diligence gaps
kp.d: Harvey is described as comparing diligence requests with data-room indexes to identify missing materials, ambiguous coverage and follow-up needs. The vendor reports that Bruchou & Funes de Rioja uses it for document categorization, risk identification and term analysis, and recounts an unspecified recent transaction where early insights freed lawyers from hours of manual review to focus on negotiation strategy.
qs: Harvey enables M&A teams to evaluate data room completeness by comparing due diligence request lists against virtual data room indexes.
This helps teams shift time away from manual cross-checking and toward substantive diligence gaps.
In a recent transaction, Harvey surfaced critical insights early in the process — freeing the team from hours of manual review so they could focus on negotiation strategy.

kp.k: Checklist generation supports execution; banking example remains hypothetical
kp.d: The author describes generating signing, closing and post-closing checklists from transaction documents, organizing deliverables, conditions, approvals and timing around deal structure. The article cites the 2025 Comerica–Fifth Third Bancorp merger, stated as a $10. 9 billion transaction, as context for complex diligence and regulatory hurdles. It proposes what Harvey could do in similar deals rather than reporting its use in that merger.
qs: M&A teams use Harvey to generate detailed signing, closing, and post-closing checklists by analyzing acquisition agreements and related transaction documents.

Real-world context: In the 2025 merger of Comerica and Fifth Third Bancorp, a $10. 9 billion transaction creating one of the largest U.S. banking franchises, legal teams faced extensive diligence and regulatory hurdles before closing.

In similar deals of this scale, Harvey could help streamline review of commercial contracts and regulatory filings, flagging material risk provisions and tracking closing conditions to help reduce the risk of key items slipping through in a complex cross-border or cross-jurisdictional review.

kp.k: Public-information synthesis builds target-company diligence profiles
kp.d: The vendor says Harvey synthesizes web information into structured profiles covering a target's business, history, industry position, ownership and recent developments. The proposed assistance includes identifying risks and areas requiring closer diligence, rather than treating a profile as the endpoint of investigation.
qs: Harvey can assist in preparing comprehensive background diligence profiles of target companies by synthesizing publicly available information into a single, structured view for the deal team.

Analyzing sources across the web, Harvey helps lawyers understand a target’s business, history, industry position, ownership structure, and recent developments — while also highlighting potential risks, red flags, or areas that may warrant closer diligence.

kp.k: Deal provisions become practical guidance for business teams
kp.d: The author describes AI translating negotiated terms into operational guidance for clients and internal stakeholders. Examples include plain-English interim operating covenants between signing and closing, explanations of earn-out calculations and disputes, indemnification limits and claims procedures, and closing responsibilities and dependencies.
qs: Rather than simply summarizing legal language, Harvey helps convert negotiated terms into practical guidance that supports day‑to‑day decision making and business execution.

For transactions with operational or timing complexity, Harvey can explain interim operating covenants in plain‑English guidance for business teams — clarifying ordinary‑course requirements, restricted actions, consent rights, and key exceptions during the period between signing and closing.

kp.k: Customer estimates ten hours saved in one week
kp.d: In a customer quotation carried by Harvey, KMSC Law partner Todd Strang reports using the product on hundreds of M&A documents to compare agreement elements, flag concerns and draft complex clauses. His estimate of 10 hours saved that week is an individual testimonial, not a measured result presented by a study.
qs: “I used Harvey to review key agreements related to an M&A transaction, comprising hundreds of documents. I was able to generate tables comparing key elements across multiple documents, flag potential issues of concern, and draft complex clauses that were beneficial to our client. I estimate Harvey saved me 10 hours just this week.”

kp.k: Disclosure assistance spans buyer analysis and seller drafting
kp.d: The article distinguishes buyer-side identification and mapping of disclosure requirements from seller-side organization, initial drafting and consistency checks. It claims these functions help buyers locate risks and negotiation opportunities, while helping sellers detect gaps, duplication and disagreement between schedules and the operative agreement before signing.
qs: On the buy side, teams use Harvey to analyze representations, covenants, and related schedules to identify required disclosures, summarize obligations, and map requirements to specific disclosure schedules.

On the sell side, Harvey assists in preparing and reviewing disclosure schedules by organizing required disclosures, drafting initial schedule content based on underlying documents, and checking for internal consistency.
Harvey can help identify gaps, duplications, and potential inconsistencies between disclosure schedules and the operative agreement — reducing the risk of omissions or misalignment before signing.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Harvey Team presents Harvey as an augmentation tool that accelerates M&A work across the deal lifecycle and redirects lawyers toward substantive judgment.
pts.d: The author's overarching claim is that embedding Harvey in existing transactional workflows saves time, surfaces risks earlier, and improves deal advice without replacing legal judgment. The article describes current uses and capabilities rather than predicting profession-wide employment changes or legal-market restructuring.

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims AI accelerates diligence, identifies missing materials and risks, and consolidates target-company information.
pts.d: Harvey is said to review large volumes of diligence documents, identify material risks and open issues, compare diligence requests with data-room indexes, and synthesize public web sources into target-company profiles. The claimed changes are earlier prioritization of high-impact issues, less manual cross-checking, and more time for substantive diligence and negotiation strategy.

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims AI speeds first-pass transaction-document review and makes precedent knowledge easier to use.
pts.d: The article says Harvey flags inconsistencies between draft agreements and terms sheets, identifies deviations from precedent, and generates issues lists with deal-specific suggested revisions. It also claims that extracting key terms across precedent agreements accelerates reporting, precedent analysis, and internal knowledge sharing.

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims AI improves deal execution through checklists and disclosure-schedule preparation and review.
pts.d: Harvey is said to extract deliverables, conditions, approvals, and timing requirements into signing, closing, and post-closing checklists. For buyers, it maps disclosure requirements and identifies risk areas; for sellers, it drafts initial schedule content and checks consistency against transaction documents. The claimed benefits include clearer execution management and fewer omissions or inconsistencies before signing.

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims AI converts complex transaction provisions into practical guidance for clients and business teams.
pts.d: The article describes plain-English explanations of interim operating covenants, earn-outs, indemnification, and closing mechanics. The asserted change is from merely summarizing legal text to producing guidance that clarifies business obligations, restrictions, responsibilities, and sequencing.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The Harvey Team supports efficiency claims with named customer examples and a workflow walkthrough.
pts.d: The article reports GSK Stockmann's initial diligence time savings of 15–20%, with savings up to 75% for unstructured data rooms. It also recounts a Bruchou & Funes de Rioja transaction in which Harvey reportedly surfaced insights early and avoided hours of manual review. A walkthrough illustrates email document capture, analysis of hundreds of contracts in Vault, and generation of a citation-backed memo. These are customer reports and a demonstration; the supplied text does not provide measurement methods, sample sizes, independent benchmarks, or quantified accuracy results.

pts.k: Todd Strang supplies a personal estimate of ten hours saved in one week, alongside reported document-review and drafting benefits.
pts.d: The ten-hour claim belongs to Todd Strang, identified as Corporate Commercial Transactions, Partner (Technology & Process) at KMSC Law, rather than to the Harvey Team as an independently measured result. His testimonial describes reviewing hundreds of M&A documents, generating comparison tables, flagging issues, and drafting clauses beneficial to a client. The evidence is his account of use and estimated time savings.

pts.k: The banking-merger example illustrates a possible application, not documented Harvey use in that transaction.
pts.d: The Harvey Team invokes the 2025 Comerica–Fifth Third Bancorp merger as context for complex diligence and regulatory work. Its claim about Harvey is expressly hypothetical and concerns similar-scale deals: streamlining document review, flagging risk provisions, and tracking closing conditions. The article does not state that Harvey was used in the cited merger. Several other capabilities are described without separate empirical support in the supplied text.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims concern present capabilities and existing use as of January 14, 2026, with task-specific conditions rather than a dated future forecast.
pts.d: The article covers early diligence through signing, closing, and post-closing. Reported savings are qualified as initial results, an upper figure for unstructured data rooms, a recent unnamed transaction, and Strang's estimate for one week. Guidance on interim covenants applies between signing and closing; disclosure checks are framed as reducing risks before signing. Benefits are presented as supporting lawyers, not eliminating legal judgment. No profession-wide adoption or displacement timetable is offered.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed benefits primarily affect transactional lawyers, buyer- and seller-side deal teams, and their clients and business stakeholders.
pts.d: Associates are said to complete first-pass review faster; partners receive more organized negotiation and risk information; senior lawyers can concentrate judgment on high-impact issues. Transaction counsel gain execution-management support. Buyer-side teams gain visibility into required disclosures and risk, while seller-side teams gain drafting and consistency-checking assistance. Clients and business teams receive more actionable explanations of negotiated obligations. Customer examples extend beyond M&A to private equity, venture capital, and real estate diligence. The source makes no specific claim about access to justice, staffing reductions, fees, or market-wide competitive effects.
